As mentioned in our first ている lesson, this construction is used to convey that someone or something is existing in a constant state of 'doing' the verb that comes before て. Here we will take a closer look at several of the verbs that will be used with ている, to express 'existing in a state of (A) having been done'.

All of these verbs would appear as the past form in English, after the initial thing has 'started', 'come', 'died', or 'gotten angry'. However, this is not the case in Japanese. In Japanese, once something is angry, it exists in the state of being angry, once something has started, it exists in the state of being ongoing, once something dies, it exists in the state of being dead, and so on.

Fun Fact

One of the easiest ways that you can tell whether a verb will use the ている form, or the past form, is to think about whether it can happen twice. Something cannot 'start' twice, so it will use ている. Something cannot die twice, so it will use ている, etc. This does not work with every verb, but will help with over 90% of the verbs that require this form.

Something has fallen and is already on the ground, so it cannot fall again. ている will be used.

The ている form describes an ongoing action or state. With verbs that describe actions over time, it functions like the English 'is...-ing,' but with state verbs, it means to be (or continue to be) in that state. For example, 食べている means 'is/am eating,' while 死んでいる means 'is/are dead' (not 'is dying').

The Verb + て form connects verbs or parts of a sentence. When an 'instantaneous' verb (one that expresses a single change in state) is combined with the existence verb いる in the ている form, it expresses an ongoing state. For example, 死んでいる means '(It) is dead.' With other verbs, ている conveys a meaning similar to the English 'is...-ing' (see ている①).

ている expresses an ongoing action or state. つづける attached to the verb stem expresses a similar meaning, but with a greater emphasis on the idea of continuation. For example, 増えている means that something is increasing or has increased, while 増えつづけている carries the additional nuance that it is continuing to increase.

The ている① form expresses completed actions or past states. Unlike English, verbs can directly modify nouns, similar to い-Adjectives. However, unless emphasizing a changing state, the past form (た) is usually preferred over ている when describing nouns. For example, 死んだネズミ ('a dead mouse') is more common than 死んでいるネズミ.

ている expresses an ongoing action or state. The ている② form is used with verbs indicating a single change in state, like 死んでいる ('is dead'), not an action. The ている③ form describes repeated or habitual actions, like 会社で働いている could mean ('I'm working for [that/this] company).
